outcome: Negami's conjecture (equivalent to showing K1,2,2,2 has no finite planar cover) remains open, but the Dec 2024 preprint by Annor, Nikolayevsky and Payne narrowed the remaining case by proving K1,2,2,2 has no planar cover of ply below 14 (a case also proved in an earlier, pre-window 2023 preprint on n<14) and that any minimal planar cover of K1,2,2,2, if one exists, must be 4-connected.
summary: Negami's 1988 conjecture ('a connected graph has a finite planar cover iff it embeds in the projective plane') is known to reduce to a single remaining case: showing the seven-vertex graph K1,2,2,2 has no finite planar cover. As of the 26 Jan 2024 Wikipedia snapshot, 31 of 32 forbidden minors had been handled, leaving only K1,2,2,2 open. Within the window, the key development is arXiv:2412.19560 ('Three Theorems on Negami's Planar Cover Conjecture', Annor, Nikolayevsky, Payne), submitted 27 Dec 2024 (revised as late as 17 Jul 2026 per the search snippet, but the first written argument is Dec 2024). It proves (i) K1,2,2,2 has no planar cover of ply below 14, and (ii) any minimal planar cover of K1,2,2,2, if it exists, must be 4-connected — both restrictions on the space where a hypothetical cover could live, narrowing but not closing the case. This is a case of the stated problem (restricting properties of a hypothetical cover of the one remaining critical graph), so it counts as `partial` progress under the case-vs-variant rule, with resolution_direction `confirmed` since the result goes in the direction the conjecture predicts (no low-ply cover exists). A closely related but pre-window preprint (arXiv:2311.01672, submitted Nov 2023, proving the same ply<14 bound) was only published in the journal Graphs and Combinatorics in Nov 2025 — per the dating rule (§6.3), the journal date is irrelevant and the first written argument (Nov 2023) predates the frozen revision, so this specific result is `open_stale` relative to the window and is not what the window-status rests on; it is mentioned only for context, since the actual within-window advance is the Dec 2024 paper providing the additional 4-connectivity result plus a re-derivation/extension of the ply bound. A second Dec 2024 preprint (arXiv:2412.04420, 'On high genus extensions of Negami's conjecture') generalizes the conjecture to arbitrary compact surfaces; this changes the stated question (different surfaces) rather than restricting it, so it is a related problem, not a case, and does not affect the status of the projective-plane conjecture as stated. A June 2026 preprint (arXiv:2606.27703) gives a new, purely combinatorial proof of an already-known special case (rotation-compatible planar covers embed in the projective plane), explicitly described by its own authors as a re-proof of a result whose 'existing proof relies on advanced algebraic and topological methods' — this is a proof-technique contribution to an already-settled sub-case, not new territory, and does not change the classification. No AI system involvement was found in any of these papers: none mention computer search, SAT solvers, computer algebra, or AI/ML tools, and none have acknowledgements referencing such tools; all are described as hand-written mathematical proofs. A mention of 'Negami's Planar Cover Conjecture' on the AI-first formal-mathematics platform ProofAtlas was also checked: it lists the problem as an open workspace with '6 routes, 4 tasks' but no completed proof or claimed result, so it does not constitute an AI contribution to this problem as of this research.
competing_reading: One could argue the ply<14 result, having first appeared (for the same bound) in a Nov 2023 preprint, is not itself a new within-window fact, so the true within-window event is only the narrower 4-connectivity result. Either way the status classification (partial, confirmed) is unchanged; I dated the event to the Dec 2024 paper since it is the first written argument establishing the 4-connected structural constraint, which is new relative to the frozen revision.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (or disproof, i.e. an exhibited finite planar cover) that K1,2,2,2 has no finite planar cover at all — closing the single remaining case — would resolve the conjecture completely.
